Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a type of
antidepressant medication
.
They’re mostly used to treat
depression
, particularly persistent or severe cases. They’re often used with a
talking therapy
like cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).
SSRIs are usually the first choice of medication for depression. This is because they have fewer side effects than other types of antidepressant.
What are SSRIs used for?
SSRIs can be used to treat many mental health conditions, including:
depression
generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)
panic disorder
severe
phobias
, like agoraphobia and social phobia
bulimia
post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
SSRIs can sometimes be used to treat other conditions, like:
premature ejaculation
premenstrual syndrome (PMS)
fibromyalgia
irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
menopause
Occasionally, they may also be prescribed to treat pain.
How SSRIs work
It’s thought that SSRIs work by increasing serotonin levels in the brain.
Serotonin is a neurotransmitter. It’s thought to have a good influence on mood, emotion and sleep.
A rise in serotonin levels can improve symptoms of depression. It can also make people more responsive to other types of treatment, like CBT.
Types of SSRIs
SSRIs are usually taken in tablet form. You may have to take 1 to 3 tablets a day. Your dose will depend on the type of SSRI you’re prescribed and the severity of your depression.
When they’re prescribed, you’ll start on the lowest possible dose. This is to reduce the risk of side effects.
You’ll usually see your doctor every few weeks when you first start taking SSRIs to discuss how well the medication is working. You can contact your doctor or pharmacist at any point if you experience any side effects.
How to take SSRIs
SSRIs usually need to be taken for 2 to 4 weeks before you’ll feel the full benefits. You may experience mild side effects early on, but it’s important that you keep taking the medication. These effects will usually wear off quickly. It may help to take your SSRI at night rather than the morning.
If you take an SSRI for 4 to 6 weeks without feeling any benefit, speak to your GP practice or mental health specialist. They may recommend increasing your dose or trying a different antidepressant.
A course of treatment usually lasts for at least 6 months. Longer courses are sometimes recommended. Some people with recurrent problems may be advised to take them indefinitely.
Missed or extra doses
It’s important not to miss any of your medication. This could make your treatment less effective.
If you do miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it’s almost time to take your next dose. In this case, you should skip the missed dose. Don’t take a double dose to make up for the one you missed.
Taking a double dose is unlikely to be harmful, but you should only do so if advised by a healthcare professional.
You should speak to your GP practice or pharmacist if you take more tablets than prescribed.
Possible side effects
The side effects of SSRIs can be troublesome at first, but most improve with time.
Common side effects
Common side effects of SSRIs can include:
feeling agitated, shaky or anxious
feeling or being sick
indigestion
diarrhoea
or
constipation
loss of appetite and weight loss
weight gain
dizziness
blurred vision
dry mouth
sweating
more than usual
sleeping problems (
insomnia
) or drowsiness
headaches
low sex drive
difficulty achieving orgasm
in men, difficulty getting or keeping an erection (
erectile dysfunction
)
Most of these side effects should improve over time. Some, like sexual problems, can persist.
Less common side effects
Less common side effects of SSRIs can include:
bruising or bleeding easily, including vomiting blood or blood in your stools (poo)
confusion
movement problems like stiffness or shaking
seeing or hearing things that aren’t real (hallucinations)
being unable to pee
Serotonin syndrome
Serotonin syndrome is a set of side effects linked to SSRIs and SNRIs. It isn’t common but it can be serious.
Serotonin syndrome occurs when levels of serotonin become too high. It’s usually triggered when you take an SSRI or SNRI with another medication (or substance) that also raises serotonin levels. For example, another antidepressant or St John’s Wort.
Symptoms of serotonin syndrome can include:
confusion
agitation
muscle twitching
sweating
shivering
diarrhoea
If you experience symptoms of serotonin syndrome, you seek immediate advice from your GP or specialist. If this isn’t possible, phone 111.
Hyponatraemia
Elderly people can have low salt levels as a side effect of taking antidepressants. This is known as hyponatraemia. It may lead to a build-up of fluid inside the cells of the body which can be dangerous.
SSRIs can block the effects of a hormone that regulates sodium and fluid levels. Elderly people are vulnerable because their fluid levels become more difficult to control.
Mild hyponatraemia can cause symptoms like:
feeling sick
headache
muscle pain
reduced appetite
confusion
If you suspect mild hyponatraemia, you should phone your GP. You may be advised to stop taking SSRIs for the time being.
Phone 999 if:
You or someone else is taking antidepressants and:
has a very high temperature (fever)
has seizures (fits)
has an irregular heartbeat (arrhythmia)
is unconscious
is feeling listless and tired
is disoriented
is agitated
Warnings and precautions
SSRIs may not be suitable if you have:
bipolar disorder
and you’re in a manic phase (a period of extremely excitable mood), although they can be useful for depressive phases
a bleeding disorder, like haemophilia
type 1 diabetes
or
type 2 diabetes
epilepsy
– SSRIs should only be taken if your epilepsy is well controlled, and they should be stopped if your epilepsy gets worse
narrow angle glaucoma
serious kidney, liver or heart problems
SSRIs can also react unpredictably with:
alcohol
large amounts of caffeine
St John’s Wort – a herbal remedy
Other medicines and SSRIs
Some medications are not suitable to take with SSRIs. This includes:
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
such as
ibuprofen
antiplatelets such as
low-dose aspirin
and
clopidogrel
theophylline – used to treat
asthma
clozapine and pimozide – used to treat
schizophrenia
and
psychosis
lithium – used to treat severe
depression
and
bipolar disorder
triptans such as naratriptan, sumatriptan and zolmitriptan – used to treat
migraines
other
antidepressants
– including tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)
You should read the patient information leaflet that comes with your medication to see if there are any medications you should avoid. Your pharmacist or GP practice should also be able to advise you.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding
SSRIs aren’t usually recommended during pregnancy, especially during the first 3 months. This is because there may be a risk to the baby.
Exceptions can be made if the risks of
depression
(or another condition) outweigh the potential risks of treatment.
If you’re pregnant and think you may be depressed, you should discuss the risks and benefits of using SSRIs with your doctor.
As a precaution, SSRIs aren’t usually recommended if you’re breastfeeding. This is because the medication may be passed to your baby in your breast milk.
SSRIs may be used if it’s thought that the benefits of treatment and breastfeeding your baby outweigh the potential risks.
Driving and using machinery
Some SSRIs can cause dizziness, drowsiness and blurred vision, particularly when you first start taking them.
If you experience these problems, avoid driving or using heavy tools and machinery.
Stopping SSRIs
You should not stop taking SSRIs suddenly, even if you feel better. Stopping suddenly can lead to withdrawal symptoms like:
stomach upsets
flu-like symptoms
anxiety
dizziness
sensations in the body that feel like electric shocks
seizures (fits)
If your GP practice or mental health specialist decides to stop your course of SSRIs, they’ll reduce the dose gradually over a few weeks.
